# Perpetual endowment (waqf, foundation, trust) (`charitable_endowment_waqf`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by property_rights_land_registry, commercial_law_contract_enforcement
- Core idea: An owner gives income-producing property (land, shops, a mill) irrevocably to a stated purpose: a school, hospital, bridge, fountain, library or relief of the poor. In a waqf, the founder names the beneficiaries and appoints an administrator to manage the dedicated assets and distribute their yield. Judges can supervise administration; the rules for changing a foundation vary across legal traditions. The service then outlives its founder and does not depend on yearly gifts or on the ruler's favour, and because endowed property is protected from confiscation and division among heirs, the rich have a strong motive to found one.
- Pitfalls:
  - Fixing the purpose forever: needs change, and a deed that cannot be altered leaves ruined schools with rich rents or the reverse; provide a way to redirect it
  - No audit of trustees: they lease the property to themselves cheaply
  - So much land passing into the 'dead hand' that rulers lose tax and later seize it (English mortmain statutes 1279, the dissolution of the monasteries, 19th c. Ottoman and Egyptian reforms)
  - Equating the waqf with the English trust: both can preserve property for beneficiaries, but their legal structures differ and direct influence is disputed
- History: egypt: c. 2500 BC – Old Kingdom tomb owners endow land to pay priests for perpetual offerings; india: from c. 1st c. AD – inscriptions record perpetual endowments (akshaya-nivi) deposited with guilds and land grants to monasteries and temples; rome: 1st–2nd c. AD – private foundations for feasts, schools and child support (Pliny the Younger at Comum); 4th–6th c. Christian piae causae with legal personality; islamic: early Islamic jurists develop waqf doctrine; a hadith relates that Umar retained land at Khaybar and assigned its yield to beneficiaries. Ottoman endowments supported families as well as schools, hospitals and fountains; china: 1050 – Fan Zhongyan's charitable estate for his lineage, which lasted into the 20th c.; Buddhist monastery endowments from the 5th c.; europe: 1264 – Merton College, Oxford, an endowed self-governing college; 13th c. the English 'use' (later trust); 1521 the Fuggerei in Augsburg, endowed housing still operating
- Read:
  - Timur Kuran, The Long Divergence: How Islamic Law Held Back the Middle East (2011)
  - Monica M. Gaudiosi, The Influence of the Islamic Law of Waqf on the Development of the Trust in England: The Case of Merton College, University of Pennsylvania Law Review 136 (1988)
